case.case_title: Amaratunga v. Sirimal and Others (Jana Ghosha Case)
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 468/92, decided on 9 February 1993

clause.text: Freedom of speech and expression including publication.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the police action in dispersing a noisy protest and assaulting the petitioner violated the petitioner's fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that his fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression was infringed when police forcibly prevented him from manifesting his protest by beating a drum and clapping during a planned nationwide protest (Jana Ghosha) against the Government, and that the police action was unjustified as it was solely because anti-Government slogans were being shouted.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the police acted lawfully under section 78(1) of the Police Ordinance to disperse the protest because they had reason to apprehend a breach of the peace, citing alleged incitement to riot and violent behavior by protesters.
key_facts: Several political parties organized a 15-minute nationwide noisy protest (Jana Ghosha) on 1 July 1992.
The petitioner, a member of the Sri Lanka Freedom Party and local council, participated by beating a drum and clapping.
Police ordered the petitioner to stop; when he did not, police assaulted him and broke his drum with a rice pounder.
Police used tear-gas and baton charges to disperse the crowd shouting anti-Government slogans.
No credible evidence of incitement to riot or violence was found; police acted solely because of anti-Government slogans.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that the right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a) includes the right to criticize the Government and political parties, and extends to expressive conduct such as drumming and clapping. Such expression cannot be denied unless it incites violence or illegal conduct.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that the police did not have objective or subjective reason to apprehend a breach of the peace at the time of dispersing the protest. The police action was a deliberate violation of the petitioner's fundamental right because it was based solely on the expression of anti-Government slogans and peaceful protest activities.
principles_established: Criticism of the Government and political parties is a permissible exercise of freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a).
Freedom of speech includes non-verbal expression such as drumming, clapping, and noisy protests.
Police may only restrict speech if there is a real apprehension of breach of peace or incitement to violence.
Unprovoked suppression of peaceful dissent violates fundamental rights and democratic principles.
precedents_cited: Police Department of Chicago v. Mosley (1972) 408 U.S. 92
Ekanayake v. A.G. S.C. Application No. 25/91

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioner's fundamental right under Article 14(1)(a) was infringed by the police action and awarded compensation of Rs. 50,000.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Compensation of Rs. 50,000 payable by the State; directions to police to respect freedom of speech and expression and not suppress peaceful protest.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, which was directly engaged by the petitioner's protest and the police's suppression of it. The court's reasoning and decision centrally relied on interpreting and applying this constitutional right.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court found that the police acted simply because anti-Government slogans were being shouted and that there was no reason to apprehend a breach of the peace, thus violating the petitioner's fundamental right under Article 14(1)(a).
